description: Investigate an anomaly in scientific data: characterize the signal, rule out instrument and processing artifacts, compare against known mechanisms, test statistical significance, and classify the finding.

steps.description: Describe the anomaly in quantitative terms: location in the dataset, magnitude, duration, shape, and context relative to the surrounding signal.

inputs.name: anomaly-description
inputs.desc: Initial qualitative description of what looks unusual

outputs.name: anomaly-profile
outputs.desc: Quantitative characterization of the anomaly

outputs.name: context-summary
outputs.desc: Summary of surrounding data behavior

process: Locate the anomaly within the dataset and extract a window around it.
Measure the anomaly's amplitude, duration, and shape parameters.
Compare the anomaly against the local baseline and global statistics.
Produce a structured profile with all quantitative descriptors.

steps.description: Check whether the anomaly could be explained by instrument malfunction, calibration drift, or sensor saturation.

inputs.name: instrument-metadata
inputs.desc: Sensor specifications, calibration logs, known failure modes

outputs.name: instrument-verdict
outputs.desc: Whether instrument error can or cannot explain the anomaly

outputs.name: instrument-evidence
outputs.desc: Supporting evidence for the verdict

process: Review calibration logs and maintenance records for the time window.
Check whether the anomaly falls outside the instrument's linear range or resolution.
Compare against known instrument failure signatures (dropout, saturation, aliasing).
Issue a verdict: instrument error ruled out, plausible, or confirmed.

steps.description: Check whether the anomaly was introduced during data processing: resampling, interpolation, filtering, normalization, or unit conversion errors.

inputs.name: processing-pipeline-description
inputs.desc: Steps used to process the raw data

outputs.name: processing-verdict
outputs.desc: Whether a processing step introduced the anomaly

outputs.name: processing-evidence
outputs.desc: Which step and what kind of artifact, if any

process: Reprocess the raw data with the anomaly window isolated.
Toggle each processing step off one at a time and check whether the anomaly persists.
Check for known artifacts of each method (Gibbs ringing from filtering, edge effects from windowing).
Issue a verdict: processing artifact ruled out, plausible, or confirmed.

steps.description: Compare the anomaly against known physical, chemical, or biological mechanisms that could produce a signal of this shape and magnitude.

inputs.name: domain-knowledge-base
inputs.desc: Catalog of known mechanisms in the relevant field

outputs.name: mechanism-candidates
outputs.desc: Ranked list of mechanisms that could explain the anomaly

outputs.name: mechanism-fit-scores
outputs.desc: How well each candidate matches the observed profile

process: Extract the anomaly's signature features (shape, timescale, amplitude, spectral content).
Search the domain knowledge base for mechanisms producing similar signatures.
Score each candidate mechanism against the observed profile.
Rank candidates by fit quality and note any that can be ruled out by auxiliary data.

steps.description: Test whether the anomaly is statistically significant against the null hypothesis of noise, drift, or expected variability.

outputs.name: significance-result
outputs.desc: p-value, confidence interval, or Bayes factor for the anomaly

outputs.name: test-details
outputs.desc: Which test was used and why, with assumptions stated

process: Select the appropriate statistical test given the data distribution and anomaly type.
Define the null hypothesis (the anomaly is a fluctuation of the background).
Compute the test statistic and its probability under the null.
Report the result with effect size and confidence bounds.

steps.description: Synthesize all evidence to classify the anomaly as confirmed real signal, probable artifact, or indeterminate requiring further data.

outputs.name: anomaly-classification
outputs.desc: Real signal, artifact, or indeterminate

outputs.name: classification-rationale
outputs.desc: Structured argument for the classification

process: Weigh instrument and processing verdicts: if either confirms an artifact, classify accordingly.
If artifacts are ruled out, check whether a known mechanism fits and significance is met.
If significance is marginal or no mechanism fits, classify as indeterminate with next steps.
Produce a structured rationale citing each line of evidence.

steps.description: Write a structured finding report: what was observed, what was ruled out, what remains, and what should happen next.

outputs.name: anomaly-report
outputs.desc: Structured finding report ready for the lab notebook or publication

outputs.name: next-steps
outputs.desc: Recommended follow-up experiments or analyses

process: Write the observation section: what, when, where, how large.
Write the investigation section: each check performed and its outcome.
Write the conclusion section: classification and confidence level.
Write the next-steps section: what additional data or experiments would resolve ambiguity.

description: Map what is known versus unknown in a research field: collect and categorize the literature, build a concept matrix, find gaps and contradictions, assess tractability, and produce a ranked gap map.

steps.description: Collect and categorize papers from a defined search: databases, keywords, date range, inclusion and exclusion criteria.

inputs.name: research-question
inputs.desc: The question or topic to map

inputs.name: search-parameters
inputs.desc: Databases, keywords, date range, inclusion/exclusion criteria

outputs.name: paper-corpus
outputs.desc: Collected papers with metadata (title, authors, year, abstract, DOI)

outputs.name: search-log
outputs.desc: Record of queries run, databases searched, and papers excluded with reasons

process: Run the defined search queries across specified databases.
Apply inclusion and exclusion criteria to screen results.
Extract metadata and abstracts for all included papers.
Log the search process for reproducibility.

steps.description: Build a concept matrix: rows are papers, columns are key concepts, cells indicate whether each paper addresses each concept and with what finding.

inputs.name: research-question
inputs.desc: The question or topic to map

outputs.name: concept-matrix
outputs.desc: Papers-by-concepts matrix with findings in each cell

outputs.name: concept-list
outputs.desc: The list of key concepts extracted from the corpus

process: Read each paper and extract the key concepts it addresses.
Consolidate concepts into a unified list, merging synonyms.
For each paper-concept pair, record the finding (supports, contradicts, partial, absent).
Produce the matrix as a structured table.

steps.description: Identify gaps in the concept matrix: concepts with few papers, conflicting findings, or missing intersections between related concepts.

outputs.name: gap-list
outputs.desc: List of identified gaps with type (sparse, conflicting, missing intersection)

outputs.name: contradiction-list
outputs.desc: Pairs of papers with conflicting findings on the same concept

process: Count papers per concept and flag concepts below a coverage threshold.
Identify concept pairs that logically intersect but have no papers addressing both.
Identify contradictions: same concept, opposite findings, similar methods.
Compile the gap and contradiction lists.

steps.description: Assess which gaps are tractable: could a new study feasibly address this gap given current methods, data availability, and ethical constraints?

inputs.name: domain-constraints
inputs.desc: Available methods, data sources, ethical and logistical constraints

outputs.name: tractability-ratings
outputs.desc: Each gap rated as tractable, partially tractable, or currently intractable

outputs.name: feasibility-notes
outputs.desc: What would be needed to address each gap

process: For each gap, identify what kind of study would fill it.
Check whether the required methods, instruments, and populations are available.
Check for ethical, legal, or logistical barriers.
Rate tractability and note what would need to change for intractable gaps.

steps.description: Rank gaps by the impact of filling them: how much would the field advance if this question were answered?

outputs.name: ranked-gaps
outputs.desc: Gaps ordered by impact, with tractability as a secondary sort

outputs.name: impact-rationale
outputs.desc: Why each gap matters if filled

process: Score each gap on theoretical importance: does it block progress on downstream questions?
Score each gap on practical importance: does it affect applications, policy, or clinical practice?
Combine impact with tractability to produce a priority ranking.
Write a one-sentence rationale for each gap's ranking.

steps.description: Produce the final gap map: a structured document showing what is known, what is not, and where the most valuable opportunities lie.

inputs.name: ranked-gaps
inputs.desc: Gaps ordered by impact and tractability

outputs.name: gap-map
outputs.desc: Structured gap map document

outputs.name: research-agenda
outputs.desc: Suggested studies to fill the top-ranked gaps

process: Organize the concept matrix into a visual or tabular overview of coverage.
Highlight the top-ranked gaps and contradictions.
For each high-priority gap, sketch the study design that would fill it.
Compile into a single document with executive summary, map, and agenda.

description: Design controls for a scientific experiment: classify variables, select positive and negative controls, plan sham or placebo conditions, design randomization and blinding, and produce the controlled protocol.

steps.description: List every variable in the experiment and classify each as independent, dependent, or confounding.

inputs.name: experiment-description
inputs.desc: What the experiment is testing and how

outputs.name: variable-registry
outputs.desc: All variables with their classification and measurement method

outputs.name: confound-list
outputs.desc: Identified confounders with their potential effect direction

process: Extract all quantities, conditions, and factors mentioned in the experiment description.
Classify each as independent (manipulated), dependent (measured), or confounding (must be controlled).
For each confound, estimate the direction and magnitude of its potential bias.
Record the measurement method and units for each variable.

steps.description: Select the positive and negative controls: what known outcome confirms the assay works, and what baseline confirms it can detect a null result.

outputs.name: positive-control-spec
outputs.desc: The positive control condition and its expected outcome

outputs.name: negative-control-spec
outputs.desc: The negative control condition and its expected outcome

process: Identify a condition known to produce a positive result with the measurement method.
Identify a condition known to produce no effect or the baseline level.
Verify that both controls use the same measurement pipeline as the experimental condition.
Document the expected outcome for each control and the criterion for pass/fail.

steps.description: Design sham, placebo, or vehicle conditions that match the experimental treatment in every way except the active ingredient.

outputs.name: sham-condition-spec
outputs.desc: The sham or placebo condition with full procedure description

outputs.name: matching-checklist
outputs.desc: Checklist confirming the sham matches on all non-active dimensions

process: List every procedural step the subject experiences in the treatment condition.
For each step, determine whether it contains the active ingredient or is incidental.
Design a sham that replicates every incidental step but omits or replaces the active ingredient.
Verify the sham is indistinguishable to the subject and the operator (if double-blinded).

steps.description: For each confounding variable, select the control strategy: hold constant, match across groups, measure and adjust statistically, or block and randomize.

outputs.name: confound-control-plan
outputs.desc: Each confounder matched to a control strategy

outputs.name: residual-confounds
outputs.desc: Confounders that cannot be fully controlled, with mitigation notes

process: For each confounder, evaluate whether it can be held constant across conditions.
If not constant, check whether subjects can be matched or blocked on it.
If matching is impractical, plan to measure it and adjust statistically.
Flag any confounders that remain uncontrolled and note the residual risk.

steps.description: Plan the randomization scheme and blinding level: simple, stratified, or block randomization; single, double, or triple blinding.

outputs.name: randomization-protocol
outputs.desc: The randomization method, blocking factors, and allocation ratio

outputs.name: blinding-protocol
outputs.desc: Who is blinded, how codes are managed, and when unblinding occurs

process: Choose a randomization method based on sample size and blocking needs.
Define the allocation ratio and any stratification factors.
Determine which parties can and should be blinded (subject, operator, analyst).
Design the code management procedure: who generates codes, where they are stored, when unblinding occurs.

steps.description: Assemble the full controlled experimental protocol: treatment groups, controls, randomization, blinding, and a checklist for execution.

outputs.name: controlled-protocol
outputs.desc: Complete experimental protocol document

outputs.name: execution-checklist
outputs.desc: Step-by-step checklist for running the experiment

process: Combine all conditions (treatment, positive control, negative control, sham) into a single protocol.
Integrate the randomization and blinding procedures.
Write the step-by-step execution checklist with decision points and abort criteria.
Review for internal consistency: every confound addressed, every group defined.

description: Establish inter-rater reliability for qualitative coding: define the scheme, train raters, run independent coding, compute agreement coefficients, identify disagreement patterns, refine the codebook, and produce the final assessment.

steps.description: Define the coding scheme: codes, definitions, inclusion and exclusion criteria for each code, and anchor examples.

inputs.name: research-question
inputs.desc: What the coding is meant to capture

inputs.name: sample-data
inputs.desc: A representative sample of the data to be coded

outputs.name: codebook-draft
outputs.desc: Complete codebook with codes, definitions, criteria, and examples

outputs.name: ambiguity-notes
outputs.desc: Known edge cases and how they should be handled

process: Read the sample data and identify the constructs to be coded.
Write a definition for each code with clear inclusion and exclusion boundaries.
Select anchor examples that illustrate clear cases and borderline cases.
Document known ambiguities and the decision rule for each.

steps.description: Train raters on the codebook using worked examples, practice rounds, and group discussion of disagreements.

inputs.name: training-dataset
inputs.desc: A small dataset with known correct codes for practice

outputs.name: training-log
outputs.desc: Record of training sessions, questions raised, and clarifications made

outputs.name: rater-readiness-assessment
outputs.desc: Whether each rater demonstrated sufficient understanding to proceed

process: Present the codebook and walk through each code with examples.
Have raters independently code the training dataset.
Compare results and discuss every disagreement as a group.
Assess readiness: raters proceed only if training agreement exceeds the threshold.

steps.description: Run the independent coding round: each rater codes the same dataset without consulting the others.

inputs.name: reliability-dataset
inputs.desc: The dataset to be coded for the reliability assessment

outputs.name: rater-code-matrix
outputs.desc: Each rater's codes for each unit of analysis

outputs.name: coding-process-notes
outputs.desc: Any difficulties raters noted during independent coding

process: Distribute the reliability dataset to each rater with blinding (no access to others' codes).
Each rater codes every unit independently using the codebook.
Collect all codes into a single matrix (units by raters).
Collect process notes on any units raters found difficult.

steps.description: Compute the inter-rater agreement coefficient: Cohen's kappa for two raters, Fleiss' kappa or Krippendorff's alpha for multiple raters.

inputs.name: code-measurement-level
inputs.desc: Nominal, ordinal, interval, or ratio level of the codes

outputs.name: agreement-coefficient
outputs.desc: The computed reliability statistic with confidence interval

outputs.name: coefficient-interpretation
outputs.desc: What the value means relative to field benchmarks

process: Select the appropriate coefficient based on number of raters and measurement level.
Compute the observed agreement and the expected agreement by chance.
Calculate the coefficient and its confidence interval.
Interpret the result using established benchmarks (e.g., Landis and Koch for kappa).

steps.description: Identify patterns in disagreements: which codes are most confused, which raters diverge most, and which data characteristics predict disagreement.

outputs.name: confusion-matrix
outputs.desc: Which codes are confused with which, and how often

outputs.name: disagreement-patterns
outputs.desc: Systematic patterns in where and why raters disagree

process: Build a confusion matrix across all rater pairs.
Identify the most commonly confused code pairs.
Check whether disagreements cluster on specific data characteristics (length, complexity, topic).
Check whether specific raters are outliers in disagreement rate.

steps.description: Refine the codebook based on disagreement patterns: clarify ambiguous definitions, add new anchor examples, split or merge codes as needed.

outputs.name: codebook-revised
outputs.desc: Updated codebook with refined definitions and new examples

outputs.name: revision-changelog
outputs.desc: What changed and why

process: For each commonly confused code pair, sharpen the boundary between them.
Add anchor examples from the actual disagreement cases.
If a code is too broad (high internal confusion), consider splitting it.
If two codes are rarely distinguished, consider merging them.

steps.description: Produce the final reliability assessment: the coefficient, the disagreement analysis, the revised codebook, and the recommendation for proceeding.

outputs.name: reliability-report
outputs.desc: Structured report suitable for a methods section

outputs.name: proceed-recommendation
outputs.desc: Whether reliability is sufficient to proceed with full coding

process: Summarize the reliability coefficient and its interpretation.
Describe the main disagreement patterns and how the codebook was revised.
State whether reliability meets the field's accepted threshold.
Recommend proceeding, re-training, or redesigning the coding scheme.

description: Determine sample size and sampling strategy for a study: specify the effect size of interest, select the test, set thresholds, compute minimum sample size, design the sampling frame, plan for attrition, and produce the sampling protocol.

steps.description: Define the minimum effect size of interest: how large a difference or association must be to matter practically or theoretically.

inputs.name: prior-evidence
inputs.desc: Previous studies or pilot data estimating the expected effect

outputs.name: target-effect-size
outputs.desc: The minimum effect size (e.g., Cohen's d, odds ratio, R-squared)

outputs.name: effect-size-justification
outputs.desc: Why this effect size matters and how it was determined

process: Review prior studies for observed effect sizes in similar questions.
Determine the smallest effect that would be practically or clinically meaningful.
If no prior data exists, use the field's conventional small/medium/large benchmarks with justification.
Document the chosen effect size, its metric, and the reasoning.

steps.description: Select the statistical test or model that will be used to test the hypothesis, based on the data type, design, and assumptions.

inputs.name: variable-types
inputs.desc: Whether variables are continuous, categorical, ordinal, count, etc.

outputs.name: selected-test
outputs.desc: The test or model chosen (e.g., two-sample t-test, mixed-effects ANOVA, logistic regression)

outputs.name: assumption-checklist
outputs.desc: Assumptions required by the test and how they will be verified

process: Classify the outcome variable's measurement level and distribution.
Determine whether the design is between-subjects, within-subjects, or mixed.
Match the data type and design to the appropriate test family.
List the assumptions and plan how to verify each one before analysis.

steps.description: Compute the minimum sample size needed to detect the target effect size with the specified power and alpha level.

inputs.name: selected-test
inputs.desc: The statistical test that will be used

outputs.name: minimum-sample-size
outputs.desc: The calculated minimum N (total and per group)

outputs.name: power-curve
outputs.desc: Power as a function of N around the minimum, showing sensitivity

process: Set alpha (typically 0.05) and power (typically 0.80 or 0.90).
Use the analytical formula or simulation for the selected test and effect size.
Compute N for the primary analysis; if multiple comparisons are planned, adjust alpha.
Generate a power curve showing how power changes with N above and below the minimum.

steps.description: Design the sampling frame: who or what is eligible, how they will be selected (simple random, stratified, cluster, multi-stage), and from what population.

inputs.name: minimum-sample-size
inputs.desc: How many subjects or units are needed

inputs.name: population-description
inputs.desc: The target population and its known structure

outputs.name: sampling-design
outputs.desc: The sampling method, strata or clusters, and selection procedure

outputs.name: eligibility-criteria
outputs.desc: Inclusion and exclusion criteria for units in the sample

process: Define the target population and its accessible subpopulation.
Choose between simple random, stratified, cluster, or multi-stage sampling based on population structure.
If stratified, define the strata and the allocation method (proportional or optimal).
Write the eligibility criteria and the procedure for selecting units.

steps.description: Plan for attrition: estimate the dropout rate, inflate the sample size accordingly, and design retention strategies.

inputs.name: minimum-sample-size
inputs.desc: The sample size before attrition adjustment

inputs.name: study-duration
inputs.desc: How long subjects will be followed or involved

outputs.name: adjusted-sample-size
outputs.desc: The enrollment target after inflating for expected attrition

outputs.name: retention-plan
outputs.desc: Strategies to minimize dropout and methods to handle missing data

process: Estimate the attrition rate from prior studies or pilot data.
Inflate the sample size using the formula: N_adjusted = N_min / (1 - attrition_rate).
Design retention strategies appropriate to the population and study length.
Plan the missing data strategy (intention-to-treat, multiple imputation, sensitivity analysis).

steps.description: Compile the complete sampling protocol: effect size, test, sample size, sampling design, attrition plan, and a recruitment timeline.

outputs.name: sampling-protocol
outputs.desc: Complete sampling protocol document

outputs.name: recruitment-timeline
outputs.desc: Estimated enrollment rate and completion date

process: Combine all components into a single protocol document.
Estimate the enrollment rate based on the sampling method and population access.
Project the recruitment timeline from enrollment rate and adjusted sample size.
Review for consistency: the test matches the design, the sample size matches the effect size.

description: Decompose a time series into interpretable components: inspect and clean the data, test stationarity, separate trend, seasonal, and residual components, detect structural breaks, forecast, and validate.

steps.description: Inspect and clean the time series: identify missing values, outliers, irregular spacing, and recording errors.

inputs.name: raw-time-series
inputs.desc: The time series data with timestamps and values

inputs.name: metadata
inputs.desc: Units, expected range, sampling frequency, known data gaps

outputs.name: cleaned-series
outputs.desc: Time series with missing values handled and outliers flagged

outputs.name: quality-report
outputs.desc: Summary of issues found and how each was handled

process: Plot the raw series and visually inspect for gaps, spikes, and drift.
Identify missing values and decide on handling (interpolation, carry-forward, or flagging).
Detect outliers using domain-appropriate criteria (not just statistical cutoffs).
Regularize the time axis if spacing is irregular.

steps.description: Test whether the time series is stationary: constant mean, constant variance, and no trend over time.

outputs.name: stationarity-result
outputs.desc: Test results (ADF, KPSS, or both) with interpretation

outputs.name: differencing-recommendation
outputs.desc: How many differences are needed to achieve stationarity, if any

process: Run the Augmented Dickey-Fuller test for the presence of a unit root.
Run the KPSS test for the null of stationarity (confirmatory, opposite null).
If non-stationary, determine the order of differencing needed.
Report the results and the recommended transformation.

steps.description: Decompose the series into trend, seasonal, and residual components using an appropriate method (classical, STL, or MSTL).

outputs.name: trend-component
outputs.desc: The extracted trend

outputs.name: seasonal-component
outputs.desc: The extracted seasonal pattern(s)

outputs.name: residual-component
outputs.desc: What remains after trend and season are removed

process: Choose between additive and multiplicative decomposition based on variance behavior.
Select the decomposition method: classical for simple cases, STL for irregular or multiple seasons.
Extract the trend, seasonal, and residual components.
Verify: trend + seasonal + residual should reconstruct the original series.

steps.description: Test for structural breaks: points where the data-generating process changed (regime shifts, level shifts, slope changes).

outputs.name: break-points
outputs.desc: Detected structural break locations with confidence intervals

outputs.name: regime-descriptions
outputs.desc: How the series differs before and after each break

process: Apply a structural break test (Chow, Bai-Perron, or CUSUM) to the residuals.
For each detected break, estimate its location and confidence interval.
Describe how the series parameters (mean, variance, trend slope) differ across regimes.
Check whether detected breaks correspond to known external events.

steps.description: Forecast the series forward with uncertainty bands: fit a model that respects the decomposition and any structural breaks.

outputs.name: forecast
outputs.desc: Point forecasts for the specified horizon

outputs.name: prediction-intervals
outputs.desc: Uncertainty bands (e.g., 80% and 95%) around each forecast point

process: Select a forecasting model that incorporates trend, season, and any regime structure.
Fit the model to the historical data (or the most recent regime if a break exists).
Generate point forecasts and prediction intervals for the desired horizon.
Check whether the forecast envelope is physically plausible.

steps.description: Validate the forecast against held-out data: compare predictions to actuals, compute accuracy metrics, and assess whether the model is trustworthy.

inputs.name: holdout-data
inputs.desc: Actual values for the forecast period, withheld during fitting

outputs.name: validation-metrics
outputs.desc: MAE, RMSE, MAPE, and coverage of prediction intervals

outputs.name: model-assessment
outputs.desc: Whether the model's forecasts are reliable enough for the intended use

process: Align forecast points with held-out actuals by timestamp.
Compute point accuracy metrics (MAE, RMSE, MAPE).
Compute interval coverage: what fraction of actuals fell within the prediction intervals.
Assess whether performance is adequate for the decision the forecast will inform.

description: Analyze a scientific network (citations, co-authorship, protein interactions, food webs): construct the graph, compute centrality, detect communities, identify structural features, and report the topology.

steps.description: Build the network graph from raw data: define nodes, edges, weights, and directionality.

inputs.name: relationship-data
inputs.desc: Raw data describing connections (e.g., citation pairs, interaction scores)

inputs.name: network-type
inputs.desc: What the nodes and edges represent

outputs.name: network-graph
outputs.desc: The constructed graph with node and edge attributes

outputs.name: graph-summary
outputs.desc: Node count, edge count, density, and whether directed or undirected

process: Parse the relationship data into a node list and an edge list.
Assign weights to edges if the data includes interaction strength or frequency.
Determine directionality: citations are directed, co-authorship is undirected.
Compute basic graph statistics: N, E, density, average degree.

steps.description: Compute centrality measures for each node: degree, betweenness, closeness, eigenvector, and PageRank.

outputs.name: centrality-table
outputs.desc: Each node with its centrality scores across all measures

outputs.name: top-nodes
outputs.desc: The highest-ranked nodes by each centrality measure

process: Compute degree centrality (raw count of connections).
Compute betweenness centrality (how often a node lies on shortest paths between others).
Compute eigenvector centrality or PageRank (importance weighted by neighbors' importance).
Rank nodes by each measure and identify the most central by each criterion.

steps.description: Detect communities or clusters in the network: groups of nodes more densely connected to each other than to the rest.

outputs.name: community-assignments
outputs.desc: Each node's community membership

outputs.name: modularity-score
outputs.desc: How well the detected communities separate from each other

process: Select a community detection algorithm appropriate for the graph size and type (Louvain, Leiden, or label propagation).
Run the algorithm and obtain community assignments.
Compute the modularity score to assess partition quality.
Check robustness by running the algorithm multiple times or with different methods.

steps.description: Identify bridges (nodes connecting otherwise separate communities) and hubs (highly connected nodes within communities).

outputs.name: bridge-nodes
outputs.desc: Nodes with high betweenness that connect different communities

outputs.name: hub-nodes
outputs.desc: Nodes with high degree or eigenvector centrality within their community

process: Identify nodes with high betweenness centrality whose neighbors span multiple communities.
Identify nodes with high within-community degree (local hubs).
Classify each node's structural role: peripheral, hub, bridge, or bridge-hub.
Note any nodes whose removal would disconnect communities.

steps.description: Test whether the network has scale-free, small-world, or other structural properties: fit the degree distribution, compute clustering and path length.

outputs.name: property-test-results
outputs.desc: Whether the network is scale-free, small-world, random, or other

outputs.name: degree-distribution-fit
outputs.desc: Best-fit distribution for the degree sequence (power law, exponential, etc.)

process: Fit the degree distribution to candidate models (power law, log-normal, exponential).
Compute the clustering coefficient and average shortest path length.
Compare clustering and path length to random graphs of the same size and density (small-world test).
Report which structural properties hold and which do not.

steps.description: Produce a publication-quality network visualization: layout, coloring by community, sizing by centrality, and labeling key nodes.

outputs.name: network-figure
outputs.desc: The rendered network visualization

outputs.name: figure-caption
outputs.desc: Caption describing the layout, coloring, and sizing conventions

process: Choose a layout algorithm (force-directed for general, circular for communities, hierarchical for DAGs).
Map community membership to node color and centrality to node size.
Label the top nodes by centrality and all bridge nodes.
Export as vector format and write the figure caption.

steps.description: Write the network analysis report: graph statistics, community structure, key nodes, structural properties, and implications for the research question.

outputs.name: network-report
outputs.desc: Structured analysis report

outputs.name: implications
outputs.desc: What the network structure means for the research question

process: Summarize the graph's basic topology: size, density, degree distribution.
Describe the community structure and the roles of key nodes.
Report which structural properties hold and what they imply (e.g., vulnerability to targeted attack if scale-free).
Connect the findings to the original research question.

description: Trace how measurement errors propagate through a calculation: catalog inputs and uncertainties, classify error types, propagate analytically or by Monte Carlo, identify dominant sources, and produce the uncertainty budget.

steps.description: Catalog every input measurement that enters the calculation, with its value, uncertainty, units, and source.

inputs.name: calculation-description
inputs.desc: The formula or procedure whose uncertainty is being assessed

inputs.name: measurement-sources
inputs.desc: Instruments, calibration records, and data sheets

outputs.name: measurement-table
outputs.desc: Each input with value, uncertainty, units, and source

outputs.name: calculation-formula
outputs.desc: The mathematical relationship between inputs and output

process: Parse the calculation to identify every input variable.
For each input, record its measured value, stated uncertainty, and units.
Note the source of each uncertainty estimate (manufacturer spec, calibration certificate, repeated measurement).
Write out the functional relationship: output = f(input_1, input_2, ...).

steps.description: Classify each input's uncertainty as Type A (evaluated by statistical methods) or Type B (evaluated by other means), and as random or systematic.

outputs.name: classified-uncertainties
outputs.desc: Each uncertainty labeled by type (A/B) and nature (random/systematic)

outputs.name: correlation-notes
outputs.desc: Any correlations between input uncertainties

process: For each uncertainty, determine whether it was derived from repeated measurements (Type A) or other information (Type B).
Classify as random (varies independently each measurement) or systematic (constant bias).
Identify any correlations: inputs measured with the same instrument or from the same calibration.
Document the probability distribution assumed for each (normal, rectangular, triangular).

steps.description: Propagate all uncertainties through the calculation: analytical method (partial derivatives) for simple cases, Monte Carlo simulation for complex or non-linear cases.

outputs.name: combined-uncertainty
outputs.desc: The total uncertainty on the output quantity

outputs.name: sensitivity-coefficients
outputs.desc: How much each input contributes to the output uncertainty

process: If the function is simple and inputs are approximately normal, use the GUM analytical method (partial derivatives).
If the function is non-linear or distributions are non-normal, use Monte Carlo propagation.
Include correlations between inputs in either method.
Compute the sensitivity coefficient (partial derivative or numerical sensitivity) for each input.

steps.description: Identify which input uncertainties contribute most to the output uncertainty and where improvement effort should be directed.

inputs.name: sensitivity-coefficients
inputs.desc: Each input's contribution to output uncertainty

outputs.name: uncertainty-ranking
outputs.desc: Inputs ranked by their contribution to the total uncertainty

outputs.name: improvement-targets
outputs.desc: Which measurements to improve and by how much to halve the output uncertainty

process: Compute each input's percentage contribution to the total variance.
Rank inputs from largest to smallest contributor.
For the top contributors, estimate how much their uncertainty would need to decrease to halve the output uncertainty.
Note whether the dominant source is Type A (can improve with more measurements) or Type B (needs better equipment or calibration).

steps.description: Compile the full uncertainty budget: a table showing each input, its uncertainty, sensitivity coefficient, contribution, and the combined result.

inputs.name: sensitivity-coefficients
inputs.desc: Sensitivity of output to each input

outputs.name: uncertainty-budget
outputs.desc: Structured budget table per GUM format

outputs.name: expanded-uncertainty
outputs.desc: Combined uncertainty multiplied by coverage factor for stated confidence level

process: Build the budget table with columns: quantity, value, standard uncertainty, sensitivity coefficient, contribution to variance.
Sum the variance contributions and take the square root for combined standard uncertainty.
Apply the coverage factor (k=2 for ~95% confidence) to get expanded uncertainty.
State the result as: value +/- expanded uncertainty with the coverage probability.

steps.description: Write the measurement uncertainty report: suitable for a calibration certificate, a methods section, or an internal quality record.

outputs.name: uncertainty-report
outputs.desc: Structured report of the uncertainty analysis

outputs.name: measurement-result-statement
outputs.desc: The final result with uncertainty in standard notation

process: Write the measurand description and the measurement procedure.
Present the uncertainty budget table.
State the measurement result: value, expanded uncertainty, coverage factor, and confidence level.
List recommendations for reducing uncertainty if the current level is insufficient.

description: Select the best model from candidates using cross-validation: define candidates, split data, train and score each, compare metrics, test for overfitting, and produce the selection report.

steps.description: Define the set of candidate models: their functional form, assumptions, complexity, and the parameters to be estimated.

inputs.name: modeling-goal
inputs.desc: What the model needs to predict or explain

inputs.name: data-description
inputs.desc: Variable types, sample size, and known data characteristics

outputs.name: candidate-list
outputs.desc: Each model with its name, form, assumptions, and complexity

outputs.name: comparison-criteria
outputs.desc: The metrics that will be used to compare models

process: List the candidate models spanning a range of complexity (simple to flexible).
For each candidate, state the functional form and the assumptions it makes.
Count the effective number of parameters as a complexity measure.
Define the comparison metrics: prediction error, information criteria, or domain-specific scores.

steps.description: Split the data for cross-validation: choose k-fold, leave-one-out, or time-series split, and create the folds.

outputs.name: fold-assignments
outputs.desc: Which observations belong to which fold

outputs.name: split-rationale
outputs.desc: Why this splitting strategy was chosen

process: Choose the CV strategy: k-fold for standard data, time-series split for temporal data, leave-one-out for very small samples.
Determine k based on sample size and computational budget.
If data has groups (e.g., patients with multiple measurements), use group-aware splitting.
Generate the fold assignments and verify that each fold has a representative distribution.

steps.description: Train each candidate model on each training fold and score it on the corresponding validation fold.

outputs.name: fold-scores
outputs.desc: Each model's score on each fold

outputs.name: training-diagnostics
outputs.desc: Any convergence warnings, singular fits, or other issues per model per fold

process: For each fold, fit each candidate model to the training portion.
Predict the validation portion and compute the comparison metric.
Record any fitting issues (non-convergence, singular Hessian, boundary estimates).
Store all scores in a models-by-folds matrix.

steps.description: Compare models across folds: compute mean and standard error of each model's score, test for significant differences, and rank.

outputs.name: model-ranking
outputs.desc: Models ordered by mean CV score with standard errors

outputs.name: pairwise-tests
outputs.desc: Statistical tests for whether the top models differ significantly

process: Compute the mean and standard error of each model's scores across folds.
Rank models by mean score (lower is better for error metrics, higher for R-squared).
Run a paired test (paired t-test or Wilcoxon signed-rank) between the top two models.
If the difference is not significant, prefer the simpler model.

steps.description: Test the selected model for overfitting: compare training performance to CV performance, check learning curves, and assess stability across folds.

outputs.name: overfit-assessment
outputs.desc: Whether overfitting is present and its severity

outputs.name: learning-curve
outputs.desc: Performance as a function of training set size

process: Compare the average training error to the average validation error for the top model.
If the gap is large, overfitting is likely: consider regularization or a simpler model.
Plot the learning curve: re-train with increasing fractions of the data and track validation error.
Check fold-to-fold stability: high variance across folds suggests sensitivity to the training sample.

steps.description: Write the model selection report: which model was chosen, why, how it performed, and what its limitations are.

outputs.name: model-selection-report
outputs.desc: Structured report suitable for a methods section

outputs.name: selected-model
outputs.desc: The chosen model with its final performance estimate and confidence interval

process: State which model was selected and the criterion used.
Report the CV performance estimate with standard error and confidence interval.
Describe the overfitting assessment and why the selected model is trustworthy (or its caveats).
Note any runner-up models and the conditions under which they might be preferred.

description: Turn raw data into publication-quality figures: select chart type, apply style guide, build the figure with proper annotations and error bars, check accessibility, generate vector output, write captions, and compile figure panels.

steps.description: Select the right chart type for the data and the message: the chart type follows from what comparison the reader needs to make.

inputs.name: data-summary
inputs.desc: Variable types, number of groups, and the intended comparison

inputs.name: message-to-convey
inputs.desc: What the figure should show the reader

outputs.name: chart-type
outputs.desc: The selected chart type with rationale

outputs.name: encoding-plan
outputs.desc: Which variable maps to which visual channel (x, y, color, size, facet)

process: Classify the comparison type: distribution, relationship, composition, trend, or spatial.
Match the comparison type and variable types to a chart family (bar, scatter, line, box, heatmap, etc.).
Check that the number of data points and groups is appropriate for the chosen type.
Define the visual encoding: which variable goes on which axis and channel.

steps.description: Apply the target journal's or venue's figure style guide: font sizes, line weights, color palette, panel labeling, and resolution requirements.

inputs.name: style-guide
inputs.desc: The journal or venue's figure specifications

outputs.name: style-config
outputs.desc: All style parameters consolidated into a config (fonts, sizes, colors, DPI)

outputs.name: compliance-checklist
outputs.desc: Checklist of style requirements and whether each is met

process: Extract font family, size for axis labels, tick labels, legends, and titles from the style guide.
Extract the required line weight, marker size, and DPI/resolution.
Select a color palette that fits the journal's constraints (print-friendly if required).
Consolidate all parameters into a reusable style config.

steps.description: Build the figure: plot the data with proper axis labels, tick formatting, error bars, statistical annotations, and legend placement.

outputs.name: draft-figure
outputs.desc: The rendered figure before accessibility and final checks

outputs.name: annotation-list
outputs.desc: All statistical annotations and callouts included

process: Create the plot with the specified chart type and encoding.
Add axis labels with units, properly formatted tick marks, and a legend if needed.
Add error bars (standard error, confidence interval, or standard deviation, stated in the caption).
Add statistical annotations (significance brackets, p-values, effect sizes) where appropriate.

steps.description: Check the figure for colorblind accessibility: simulate the three common forms of color vision deficiency and verify all distinctions survive.

outputs.name: accessibility-result
outputs.desc: Pass or fail with specific issues identified

outputs.name: fix-recommendations
outputs.desc: Alternative colors, patterns, or markers to resolve issues

process: Simulate deuteranopia, protanopia, and tritanopia views of the figure.
Check whether all data series remain distinguishable in each simulated view.
If any series merge, recommend alternative colors, dashing patterns, or marker shapes.
Verify that the figure does not rely solely on color for any critical distinction.

steps.description: Export the figure as vector format (PDF, SVG, or EPS) at publication resolution, with fonts embedded and no rasterization of line art.

outputs.name: vector-figure-file
outputs.desc: The exported vector file ready for submission

outputs.name: export-log
outputs.desc: Format, resolution, file size, and any warnings

process: Set the output format based on journal requirements (PDF preferred, SVG or EPS as fallback).
Embed all fonts to prevent substitution on the reviewer's or typesetter's machine.
Ensure line art is not rasterized: lines, text, and axes should remain vector.
Check the file size against the journal's upload limit.

steps.description: Write the figure caption: title line, description of what is shown, definition of error bars and statistical annotations, and sample sizes.

outputs.name: figure-caption
outputs.desc: The complete caption text

outputs.name: caption-checklist
outputs.desc: Whether the caption covers all required elements (n, error bar definition, significance threshold)

process: Write a title line that states what the figure shows, not what the reader should conclude.
Describe the data: what each axis, color, and symbol represents.
Define the error bars (SEM, 95% CI, SD) and the significance threshold for any annotations.
State the sample size for each group or condition.

steps.description: Compile multiple sub-figures into a multi-panel figure: align axes, assign panel labels (A, B, C), and ensure consistent styling across panels.

outputs.name: compiled-panel
outputs.desc: The final multi-panel figure

outputs.name: panel-caption
outputs.desc: Caption with sub-panel references (A) ..., (B) ...

process: Arrange panels in the specified layout (rows, columns, or custom grid).
Align shared axes across panels so values are directly comparable.
Add panel labels (A, B, C) in a consistent position and size.
Verify that font sizes, line weights, and colors are identical across all panels.
